Delivery & Technology · Requirements & Specification

Acceptance criteria and error cases

How will we know each requirement is met — including when things go wrong?

1A Tuesday in January

On the morning of 13 January 2026, Meera Kulkarni printed a spreadsheet she did not want to read. She is the product manager for recurring collections at Prithvika Payments, a Bengaluru company that sells payment infrastructure to about 900 mid-market merchants — gyms, tuition chains, housing societies, a few insurance brokers. Her team had shipped UPI AutoPay mandates in November: a merchant sets up a standing instruction once, and every month Prithvika's system asks the customer's bank to debit the agreed amount automatically.

The build had gone cleanly. The requirement in the PRD read: "A merchant can collect a recurring payment from a customer on the agreed date without the customer re-authorising each time." Beneath it sat a single line of acceptance criteria: "Debit succeeds and merchant sees the payment in the settlement report." Engineering shipped exactly that. It worked.

By 13 January there were 6,200 active mandates. In the December cycle, 11.3 per cent of debit attempts did not succeed — roughly 700 attempts. Nobody had written down what should happen to those 700. The system, left to its own devices, retried them the next morning. For most, this was harmless. For 119 attempts, the customer's bank had not replied at all within Prithvika's 30-second timeout, so the platform recorded a failure and retried — and for 27 of those, the bank had in fact debited the customer the first time. Twenty-seven customers were debited twice, an average of ₹2,450 each, ₹66,150 in all. Prithvika's support desk logged 412 tickets in nine days. Two merchants, including a Pune tuition chain with 1,400 students on mandates, asked to move to a competitor.

None of this was a bug in the sense an engineer would recognise. The code did what the specification said. The specification simply said nothing about the 11.3 per cent, and silence in a specification is not neutrality — it is a decision, made later, by whoever happens to be writing the code at the time. Meera's decision that Tuesday was how much of the error space to write down before the team began the retry-and-refund work scheduled for February, and what it would cost her in cycle time to do it.

2The idea, stated precisely

Acceptance criteria are the set of observable conditions, agreed before the work begins, under which everyone concerned will accept that a requirement has been met. Two properties do the work. They are observable: they describe something a person or a test script can look at and report, not an internal intention. And they are binary: each one resolves to met or not met, with no third answer that depends on who is holding the laptop.

Error cases are the branches of the same requirement in which the core scenario does not complete — and, crucially, the specified behaviour for each branch. An error case is not a note that something might fail. It is a statement of what the system must then do: what the user sees, what state the system lands in, what it records, and whom it tells.

The lineage is older than software product management. Acceptance testing arrived with contract programming in the 1960s and 1970s, where a buyer would not pay until agreed tests passed on their own premises; the idea that acceptance belongs to the customer rather than the builder is inherited directly from that commercial arrangement. Ivar Jacobson's use cases, developed at Ericsson and published in 1987, contributed the structural insight that matters most here: a use case has a basic flow and a set of alternate and exception flows, and the exception flows are part of the specification, not an appendix to it. Extreme Programming in the late 1990s — Kent Beck and Ward Cunningham — turned this into per-story "customer tests" written before the code. Dan North's Behaviour-Driven Development, from about 2003, gave the world the Given/When/Then sentence that most teams now use as their default grammar.

"A requirement isn't done when the code runs. It's done when we can name the one thing that must be observably true when it works — and what the system must do in each of the ways it can fail."

That is the sentence Meera could say in a planning meeting without sounding either pedantic or glib. It contains the whole argument of this page: the core scenario is one line, and the error cases are the rest of the specification.

3How it actually works

The mechanics are a sequence, and the steps practitioners skip are always the same ones. Step one is to state the requirement as a behaviour with an actor: not "build retry logic" but "when a scheduled debit does not succeed, the merchant and the customer each end up in a defined position within a defined time." Step two is to name the core scenario — exactly one. If a requirement seems to have three happy paths, it is three requirements wearing one hat.

Step three is where the craft lives. You walk the core scenario one step at a time and, at each step, ask a mechanical question: what can this step return other than success? Not "what might go wrong", which invites imagination and produces whatever the most anxious person in the room happens to fear. The mechanical question produces a repeatable enumeration, because each step has a finite set of non-success returns: the input can be invalid, a precondition can be unmet, the actor can be unauthorised, a dependency can refuse, a dependency can fail to answer at all, the same request can arrive twice, a limit can be hit, or the state may already have moved on since the request was made.

Step four is the step most teams leave implicit, and it is the difference between a list of worries and a specification. For each error case you must decide behaviour in four separate registers, because they are genuinely independent choices. What does the user see — and which user, since a merchant and an end customer are not the same person. What state does the system land in, including any money or inventory already committed. What is recorded — the event, the log line, the metric the team will use to find out how often this happens. And who is notified, actively, without having to go looking.

Step five is to write each criterion so that two competent people, observing the same build independently, would write the same verdict. This is the only quality test that matters and it is cheap to run. "The error message is clear" fails it. "On a declined debit the customer receives an SMS within 5 minutes naming the merchant, the amount and the retry date" passes it.

Step six is to mark which criteria block release and which do not — otherwise every criterion becomes a launch veto and the team quietly stops writing them. Step seven, which almost nobody does and which Meera adopted, is to keep a visible list of the error cases the team has deliberately decided not to specify this time, with a default clause covering them. That converts silence into a recorded decision.

4The worked example, line by line

Meera took the December cycle and decomposed the 700 non-successful attempts by cause. The arithmetic is worth following because it changes which criteria are worth writing.

Of the 119 ambiguous attempts, 27 (22.7%) were later found to have succeeded at the bank after Prithvika had recorded failure and retried. Average ticket ₹2,450; double-debited value ₹66,150. Support: 412 tickets over nine days at a fully-loaded ₹165 per ticket = ₹67,980, plus 27 manual refunds at roughly 40 minutes each.

Read the table as a prioritisation instrument, not a post-mortem. The largest bucket by volume — 427 insufficient-funds cases — is the least dangerous, because the money demonstrably did not move and the only question is when to try again and what the customer is told. The 119 ambiguous cases are 17 per cent of failures but produced essentially all of the financial damage and most of the 412 tickets, because they are the only bucket in which the system's belief about the world can be wrong.

Now change one input. Prithvika's bank partners degrade during high-traffic weekends; in the sample from Diwali week the no-reply share had run at 34 per cent rather than 17. Hold the other assumptions constant and the arithmetic moves: 700 failures × 34% = 238 ambiguous attempts, and at the same 22.7 per cent wrongly-recorded rate, 54 double debits rather than 27, or about ₹132,300 in a single cycle. The insufficient-funds bucket shrinks proportionally to roughly 320 attempts and costs nothing extra.

The consequence is not simply "the problem is bigger." It is that the identity of the most valuable acceptance criterion changes. At 17 per cent, the criterion Meera would have written first is the customer-facing one — the message, the retry date, the tone. At 34 per cent, the first criterion must be the boring infrastructural one: every debit request carries an idempotency key, and a request that is retried with the same key must never result in a second debit; any attempt with no reply must be reconciled against the bank's own record within 90 minutes and its status resolved before any retry is attempted. One criterion, unglamorous, no user interface, and it removes 54 double debits a cycle. Sensitivity to a single input reordered the specification.

5Nuances a learner must acquire

Criteria are not test cases, and confusing them costs you the engineer's goodwill

An acceptance criterion states what must be true. A test case states how you will check it, with which data, in which environment. One criterion — "a retried debit with the same idempotency key never produces a second debit" — may require eleven test cases, including a nasty one involving two servers racing. The product manager owns the criterion; quality engineering owns the tests. A PM who writes test cases is doing someone else's job badly and will be resented for it; a PM who writes no criteria has outsourced product policy to a test plan.

The happy path is a scenario; the error space is a distribution

Meera's 700 failures were not seven hundred surprises. They fell into four buckets with stable proportions that any competent analyst could have estimated before launch by asking the bank partner what its decline mix looked like. Treat the error space as something you measure and forecast, not something you imagine. The corollary is that you can rank error cases by expected annual incidence and expected cost per incident and specify in that order, which is exactly what Exhibit 1 does.

Failure and ambiguity are different outcomes

Most engineers and almost all specifications model two outcomes, success and failure. Distributed systems have three: success, failure, and no answer. The third is not a rare corner — at Prithvika it was 119 events a month — and it is the only one in which the system's record and reality can diverge. Whenever a requirement crosses a network, a payment rail, a partner API or a hardware device, ask explicitly what happens when the other side never answers. The presence or absence of that sentence in a PRD is the fastest way to judge whether the author has shipped anything transactional before.

Criteria constrain behaviour; they should not dictate implementation

"Retry three times with exponential backoff using the Kafka consumer" is not an acceptance criterion; it is a design decision smuggled into a requirement, and it robs engineering of the freedom to solve the problem better. The right form is outcome and deadline: no second debit, reconciled within 90 minutes. The exception is real and important — where the mechanism itself is externally mandated by a regulator, a network scheme or a contract, the mechanism is the requirement and must be written as such.

Every error case encodes a policy about who bears a cost

When a debit is ambiguous and the customer may have paid twice, someone absorbs the loss while it is resolved: the customer waits three days for a refund, the merchant absorbs a chargeback, or Prithvika credits the amount immediately and recovers it later. That is not an engineering choice. It is a commercial decision about which relationship the company is willing to strain, and if the product manager does not make it in writing it will be made by default inside a catch block by an engineer at 11 p.m.

Completeness is unreachable; bounded incompleteness is the goal

You will never enumerate every error case, and a team that tries will spend three weeks specifying the behaviour of events that occur twice a decade. The professional posture is not completeness but explicit coverage: specify the cases you have chosen, state a default for everything else ("any unclassified failure holds the attempt in pending, alerts on-call, and never auto-retries"), and keep a short visible list of what you knowingly left out. Gaps you have named are risks; gaps you have not named are incidents waiting for a date.

What criteria cannot tell you, however well written

Acceptance criteria answer "is the requirement met". They are silent on whether the requirement was worth building, whether customers want it, whether the experience is good rather than merely correct, and whether the feature interacts destructively with something built two years ago by a team that has since disbanded. A build can pass every criterion and be a commercial failure. Criteria are a verdict instrument, not a judgement instrument, and treating a green test board as evidence of product success is one of the most common category errors in delivery organisations.

Timing changes their function entirely

Written before estimation, acceptance criteria are a negotiation device: engineering sees the real scope, the estimate moves from nine days to fourteen, and the team chooses knowingly. Written after the build, the identical words become an accusation, and the conversation turns into a scope dispute nobody wins. The text is the same; the timing determines whether it is a design tool or a weapon.

6How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the volumes are large and the value of each event is small, so the dominant question is recovery without user action. The best consumer error handling is invisible: the app retries, reconciles and never shows a code. Criteria therefore concentrate on silent recovery, on the wording and timing of the one message that does reach the user, and on not blaming them. A consumer team that writes "display error 4032" has misunderstood its own product.

In B2B and enterprise the criteria are frequently contractual. Acceptance may literally trigger a payment milestone or a user-acceptance-testing sign-off, so the wording is read adversarially by people whose job is to read it adversarially. Permission and role errors dominate the error space — what an approver sees when a maker has exceeded a limit — and the audit record is not a nicety but often a criterion in its own right, because a regulated customer must be able to reconstruct who did what.

Marketplaces have the structural complication that every error case has two audiences with opposed interests. When a supplier cancels, the buyer's experience and the supplier's penalty are the same event seen from two ends, and the criteria must specify both sides and be mutually consistent — the commonest marketplace defect is a message to one side that contradicts what the other side was told.

By stage the pathologies invert. Early-stage teams write too few criteria, which is usually forgivable except on the money-touching and irreversible paths, where it never is. Large organisations write too many: sixty criteria of which perhaps nine matter, attached to a sign-off ritual that detects nothing because no human reads sixty lines with attention. The mature move in a large firm is not more criteria but a ruthless distinction between the blocking few and the documented rest.

7Common mistakes and their cheapest diagnostics

The first is criteria that are not verdicts. The symptom is visible from outside: two people watch the same demo and disagree about whether it is done. The underlying misunderstanding is that criteria describe quality rather than deliver a ruling. The cheapest diagnostic takes ninety seconds — hand the criterion to two people, ask each to write "met" or "not met" without conferring, and see whether they match.

The second is delegating the error space to engineering as "standard error handling". The symptom appears about a month after launch as a proliferation of support macros — canned replies the support team wrote because customers kept asking the same unanswerable question. Read the macros written in the thirty days after any launch: each one is an acceptance criterion the product manager failed to write, priced at the cost of the tickets that produced it.

The third is criteria that are a transcription of the user interface. The symptom is that criteria churn every time a designer moves a button, and the team stops maintaining them. The misunderstanding is confusing the interface with the behaviour. The diagnostic is a single question: would this criterion survive a complete redesign? If not, it is describing a screen, not a requirement.

The fourth is the one that cost Prithvika ₹66,150 and two accounts: no specified behaviour for in-flight or ambiguous state. The symptom is a reconciliation spreadsheet maintained by hand, usually by the most junior person in operations. The diagnostic is to ask, of any requirement that crosses a system boundary, what the product does if the other side never answers. A team that cannot answer in one sentence has not specified the requirement, whatever the length of the document.

8What good looks like

Three floors up from Meera, the risk platform team at Prithvika had shipped merchant-onboarding checks in September with what looked like an unremarkable document. Its requirement section ran to a page; its acceptance section ran to four. The core scenario occupied six lines. The remainder enumerated nineteen error cases in the four-register grid, of which seven were marked blocking and twelve were explicitly marked "documented, non-blocking, behaviour defaults to hold-and-alert". A final short list named five cases the team had decided not to handle in version one, each with a sentence explaining why and an owner. The estimate rose from three weeks to four and a half when engineering read it, and the team accepted that trade knowingly. In four months of operation the feature generated eleven support tickets. No spreadsheet was maintained by hand.

9What Meera decided

Meera did not try to specify the whole error space. She ranked the four buckets by expected cost rather than volume, and wrote full four-register criteria for the ambiguous-reply case and the revoked-mandate case — the two where the system's belief could be wrong or where money moved without anyone intending it. For insufficient funds, the largest bucket, she wrote three lines and a default. For everything unenumerated she wrote a hold-and-alert default and a list of six named gaps with owners. The February estimate moved from nine days to thirteen, and she took the four days to her director with Exhibit 1 in hand, arguing that ₹66,150 a cycle and two at-risk merchants was a better comparison than four days of engineering.

What to learn next follows from what this page has left open. Edge cases, states and permissions extends the enumeration from failures to state machines and role-based behaviour, which is where B2B error spaces actually live. Requirements traceability is what keeps a criterion connected to the test that proves it when the feature is modified eighteen months later by someone who has never met Meera. And definition of done raises the level from a single requirement to the team's standing contract about what shipping means.

Two questions to sit with. First: in the last feature you shipped, what was the system's behaviour when a dependency did not answer — and if you do not know, who decided it? Second: if an acceptance criterion encodes a policy about who absorbs a cost, what does it say about an organisation that lets those criteria be written after the code is built?

case20v1-req.acceptance:
Lagat Pay: What Does "Done" Mean for Auto-Settle?

A teaching case on acceptance criteria and error cases

1. Opening

At 9.40 pm on Tuesday 20 October 2026, Varinder Ehlawat was still at his desk in Lagat Pay's office in Chandigarh's Industrial Area, Phase II. The specification for a feature called Auto-Settle was open in one window and a message from New Jersey in the other. Ehlawat, the company's head of product, had until five o'clock the next afternoon, Wednesday 21 October, to tell his engineers what "done" meant. Building would start on Thursday 22 October.

Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November. In the fortnight before it, India's distributors close their books and chase every outstanding rupee from retailers. The requirement on his screen read: "Retailer approves a UPI AutoPay mandate; Lagat debits the agreed amount on the due date." Everyone who had read it believed they understood it, and the Pune test team had already asked for the test cases. Ehlawat had spent the evening with six weeks of pilot data, and was no longer sure.

2. Company background

Lagat Pay was founded in 2019 by two former bank operations managers. It sells collection software to FMCG distributors, the intermediaries who carry biscuits, soap and dairy products from manufacturers such as Amul to kirana retailers, who usually buy on thirty days' credit. By September 2026 Lagat served 3,800 distributors, mostly in Punjab, Haryana, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh. It had processed ₹2,400 crore of retailer payments in FY26 and reported revenue of ₹41 crore. Retailers paid through a Lagat link that opened any UPI app.

The company employed 210 people: product and finance in Chandigarh, engineering in Bengaluru, a test team in Pune, customer success in Singapore and enterprise sales in New Jersey. Razorpay and PhonePe sold payment links to the same distributors, and ledger apps such as Khatabook sat on the retailer's phone. All of them waited for the retailer to pay. Lagat's bet was that a scheduled pull would shorten collection delays and let it charge distributors a higher monthly subscription. Early distributors had asked for the feature in the same breath as they asked for faster reconciliation, since a late payment forces them to carry stock on their own money.

NPCI's UPI AutoPay allows a customer to approve a mandate once. The merchant must then send a pre-debit notification at least 24 hours before each debit, and the retailer's bank may decline or time out at any point. RBI's rules on recurring payments apply throughout.

3. The situation

The pilot ran for six weeks to 16 October with 14 distributors and 212 retailers, and scheduled 1,600 debits. Its only written acceptance criterion was "the debit succeeds and the distributor's ledger shows paid". Exhibit 1 sets out the outcomes. Of the 1,600 debits, 1,312 succeeded cleanly and 288 did not.

In 52 debits the bank timed out without answering, and the system waited four hours and sent the request again. Separately, in 11 further cases a first request that had timed out had in fact gone through, and the retailer was debited twice. Refunds took six days on average. In 29 of the 52 timeouts, the distributor's dashboard showed "Failed" even though the money might already have left the retailer's account.

Vivian Eng, who runs customer success from Singapore and starts her day 2.5 hours ahead of Chandigarh, had sent her ticket analysis overnight. Her seven-person desk had improvised every reply, and she wrote that no two agents had told a retailer the same thing about a pending debit. Veenu Ehluwalia, the engineering manager in Bengaluru, reported that her engineers had built three different retry rules, each defensible, because nothing said which was wanted.

Vishwajeet Eshar, the sales head, had written at noon his time, 9.30 pm in Chandigarh, because New Jersey is 9.5 hours behind India until clocks change on 1 November. A Dubai-headquartered snacks exporter whose Indian distribution arm serves 1,150 retailers across Punjab, Haryana and Delhi had signed a ₹3.2 crore annual contract on 29 September. His message said the client expected Auto-Settle live on 2 November. Ehlawat then opened the contract, which promised the feature "to the Client's retailers before Diwali".

Pune had so far written tests only for the success case; the rest, its lead said, would be "whatever the specification tells us to check". Planners expected about 8,000 scheduled debits across a launch cohort of 60 distributors in the first thirty days, assuming Diwali-season dues run about 1.6 times the pilot's per-distributor pace. Veenu had priced three ways of writing the requirement (Exhibit 2), and Exhibit 3 places their release dates against the festival.

4. The people

Vishwajeet Eshar, head of sales, Jersey City. He joined Lagat from a global payments firm in 2024, works Indian evenings to keep overlap with Chandigarh, and carries the Dubai relationship. He wants 2 November, because the client's own finance team has planned its Diwali collections around it and because Razorpay and PhonePe already sell payment links to distributors like it.

Veenu Ehluwalia, engineering manager, Bengaluru. She leads five engineers and the Pune test team. The pilot cost her team two weeks of rework, and she says she can estimate and test only what is written down in a form a tester can run.

Vivian Eng, customer success lead, Singapore. Her desk takes the calls when a retailer sees money leave without a receipt. She wants to know before launch what to tell people in each situation, and what the dashboard will say.

Ehlawat had written the one-line requirement himself in August, when Auto-Settle was a six-week experiment rather than a product, and he now had to decide how much more it needed before real retailers' money moved through it.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: ship the happy path. Write one criterion, that the debit succeeds and the ledger shows paid. Every other outcome produces the same screen, "Payment could not be completed". It costs five engineer-weeks and meets Eshar's 2 November date. About 1,440 of the 8,000 expected debits would reach that screen.

Option B: specify every outcome. Write criteria and a test for all five failure categories and the 14 bank response codes seen in the pilot logs. It costs 19 engineer-weeks and releases on 24 November, sixteen days after Diwali.

Option C: specify the main categories. Write criteria for insufficient balance, revoked mandate, timeout and duplicate debit. The other 21 would share one generic criterion. It costs eight engineer-weeks and releases on 5 November.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. From Exhibit 1, which outcomes are most frequent, and which matter most to a retailer or a distributor regardless of frequency?
  2. Write the acceptance criteria, in given/when/then form, for the bank-timeout case. What must the system do, what must the retailer and distributor see, and how would the Pune team test it?
  3. Which failure categories need written, testable behaviour before the build starts, and which can share a generic criterion? What rule are you using to draw that line?
  4. Which option should Ehlawat choose by Wednesday, and what should he tell Eshar, Ehluwalia and Eng?

8. A note for the learner

An acceptance criterion converts "the requirement is met" into something a tester, a support agent and a distributor would observe identically. Written for the success path alone, it leaves every other outcome to whatever each engineer assumed. In the pilot that was 288 of 1,600 debits, or 18 per cent. The discipline is to list the outcomes, give each an observable behaviour, and spend the effort where the behaviour decides whose money sits where.

One defensible path is Option C. Ehlawat writes criteria for the four named categories and one catch-all: no second debit, a visible "could not complete" message with a reference number, and a status check the next morning. A sample timeout criterion reads: given a debit request unanswered by the bank after 90 seconds, when the retry timer fires, then no second request is sent until the bank's status query returns, and the distributor sees "Awaiting bank", not "Failed". Ehluwalia can estimate that, and Pune can test it.

Timeout and duplicate debits together account for 315 of the 8,000 expected debits, or ₹78.75 lakh in transit with an uncertain status. The extra 11 engineer-weeks of Option B would buy criteria for 105 debits, ₹26.25 lakh at the pilot's mean amount, which the catch-all would already cover. The 5 November release sits inside the contract's "before Diwali" wording, so Ehlawat can offer Eshar a date that the contract supports. The 105 expected unspecified debits are a stated, bounded risk.

Manzil Technologies: What Acceptance Means

Pune, Sunday 18 October 2026. A two-page certificate, eighty-seven error cases and a bank that does not always answer.

I. The night before

A little after nine on Sunday evening, 18 October 2026, the fourth floor of Manzil Technologies' office on Baner Road in Pune held one person. Yudhvir Gakhal, senior director of product for the collections platform, had come in to read a document he had read four times already, and to decide what to say about it at eleven next morning.

The document ran to two pages: the acceptance certificate for Manzil's first contract outside India, a recurring-collections platform for Mirdif Lease Finance, a Dubai consumer and auto lender with 1,74,000 active direct-debit mandates. Signed, it released the third milestone, AED 13,86,000, or ₹3.32 crore at the contract rate. Unsigned by Friday 23 October, it would open a board meeting at which Manzil's Series B term sheet was also down for discussion.

What had stopped him was not in the certificate. It was in a nine-day-old memo from Toronto reporting that in September Manzil's India platform had debited some customers twice, that the cause had gone unidentified until October, and that the mechanism which found it did not exist in the system Mirdif was about to go live on. The certificate did not mention error handling. Nor did the happy-path criteria it referred to.

II. How Manzil got here

Yashnoor Garcha started Manzil in 2017 with a classmate who left in 2021, turning small lenders' instalment files into NACH debit batches and handing back the rejections. By 2026 it ran 41 client programmes, 1.18 crore active mandates and 1,02,60,000 debit attempts in September alone. Revenue for the year to 31 March 2026 was ₹64.2 crore, of which ₹21.8 crore was transaction fees; at ₹2.90 per successful debit, September's fees came to ₹2.44 crore, an annualised ₹29.3 crore.

One decision from 2019 shaped everything after. To win Morinda Credit, a Chandigarh consumer-durables lender and still among Manzil's largest India programmes, Garcha took a master services agreement drafted by the client's counsel. It uses the word "acceptance" forty-one times and defines it once: successful completion of the Client UAT Suite. The same quarter, engineering chose one mandate state machine for everybody, with each client's exception handling in a per-programme spreadsheet called the behaviour sheet. That pairing won 41 programmes in seven years. It also means Manzil has no central answer to what the platform should do when a bank does not reply.

III. The industry

Recurring payments in India are a regulated utility on two rails. NACH and e-NACH, operated by NPCI, carry lenders' instalments; UPI Autopay carries subscriptions for firms like Zomato, Swiggy and Zerodha. Since 2022 an e-mandate above ₹15,000 needs additional factor authentication at every debit under the Reserve Bank's recurring-payments framework, and every debit needs a pre-debit notification twenty-four hours in advance. Razorpay, PhonePe, Paytm and BillDesk all sell mandate management, and most lenders keep two processors live.

Two regulatory facts bear on Mirdif. The Reserve Bank's payment-data storage directive requires India payment data to be held only in India, so the UAE deployment is a separate stack in a Gulf region with no pipeline back to Pune. And the UAE Direct Debit System, which Al Etihad Payments runs for the Central Bank of the UAE, returns its own reject reasons on its own calendar. Manzil also runs a four-person sales office in New Jersey, where two prospects have asked for the Mirdif annexe as a template.

IV. The situation in detail

On 12 February 2026 Manzil and Mirdif signed, then spent two days in a Dubai room writing acceptance criteria. The output was 28 happy-path criteria across eight requirement groups, plus 31 exceptions in free text marked best effort, per behaviour sheet. Expected behaviour was written down for 22 of the 31. The matrix became Annexure C, signed on 20 March. Three names are in its revision history: a Manzil business analyst, a Manzil quality engineer and Mirdif's project manager.

On 24 April a quality engineer in Pune introduced an E-code taxonomy; the 31 free-text exceptions were recoded under it and 29 added, taking the list to 60. A second tranche on 15 July added 27 more, for 87. Behaviour was filled in for 14 of the new ones and for none of the old gaps. Both tranches went by email; neither was executed as an amendment.

UAT cycle three ran from 3 August to 25 September. On 27 August Morinda Credit's head of collections sent Pune 218 customers who had complained of being debited twice in July. The cause, confirmed on 9 October by a sweep run from Toronto, was requirement R-04: where a sponsor bank returns no final status, 29 of the 41 behaviour sheets instruct the platform to present the debit again after ninety minutes, and some of those banks had already posted the money. Acceptance criteria and error cases

The core scenario is one line. The specification is what you write about the other eleven per cent.

1Two decisions, one week apart

On 3 March 2026, Kavya Menon sat in a conference room in Hyderabad with two clinical pharmacists and her engineering lead, arguing about a sentence. Kavya is group product manager at Pushpanjali Health Systems, which sells a hospital information platform to private hospital chains; the module under discussion was an AI-assisted drug-interaction alert that reads a doctor's prescription and warns the pharmacist when two drugs should not be dispensed together. The customer, an eleven-hospital chain across Telangana and Karnataka, had scheduled user-acceptance testing for 20 April, and ₹2.1 crore of the contract's milestone payment was attached to sign-off. The chain's chief pharmacist had proposed an acceptance criterion of one sentence: "The system must not miss a clinically significant interaction." Kavya's engineering lead, Farhan Qureshi, had spent forty minutes explaining why the team could not sign it, and the room had heard him as evasive rather than truthful.

Two days later and 600 kilometres away, Rohan Deshmukh faced a smaller decision with the same shape. Rohan is a product manager at Prithula Rides, a Pune company running a two-sided marketplace for intercity car travel: passengers book a seat, independent drivers accept the trip. Prithula handles roughly 41,000 trips a month across about 3,100 active drivers. In February, 3.8 per cent of accepted trips — 1,558 of them — were cancelled by the driver after acceptance, and 640 of those cancellations happened after the passenger had already left home for the pickup point. The requirement on Rohan's desk was to "handle driver cancellations gracefully." Nobody had yet written down what the passenger sees, what the driver sees, who pays the difference when the replacement trip costs more, and whether the two screens are permitted to disagree. Twenty-two per cent of Prithula's cancellation support tickets in January contained some version of the sentence "my app said one thing and the driver said another."

These are not two problems. They are the same problem at different points on a single axis, and the argument of this page runs along that axis: an acceptance criterion is a decision about who bears the cost of a system's imperfection, written in a form that can be checked. The core scenario is trivial to specify and rarely where value or risk lives. Everything that distinguishes a competent specification from an expert one happens in the error cases — including, as Kavya's room discovered, whether the error case can be eliminated at all.

2The idea, its history, and who disagrees about it

Acceptance criteria are the conditions, agreed before build, under which the parties concerned will accept that a requirement has been met. Two properties are load-bearing. They must be observable — describing evidence that can be examined rather than intent that must be trusted. And they must be decidable — each resolves to met or not met, without depending on who is holding the laptop. Error cases are the branches in which the core scenario does not complete, together with the required behaviour for each: what each affected party sees, what state the system lands in, what is recorded, and who is told.

The intellectual history has four distinguishable roots, and the schools that descend from them still disagree in ways that matter. The oldest is commercial: acceptance testing in 1960s and 1970s contract programming, where a buyer did not pay until an agreed test suite passed on the buyer's premises. That lineage — visible today in enterprise UAT, in IEEE 830-style requirements specification, and in the V-model — treats acceptance as a commercial event owned by the customer. The second root is structural: Ivar Jacobson's use cases, developed at Ericsson and published in 1987, which gave us basic flow, alternate flows and exception flows, and with them the proposition that failure paths are part of the specification rather than an appendix. The third is the Extreme Programming tradition of the late 1990s — Kent Beck, Ward Cunningham — which pulled acceptance tests forward to before the code and made them per-story; Dan North's Behaviour-Driven Development from around 2003, later systematised in Gojko Adzic's Specification by Example (2011), added the Given/When/Then grammar and the claim that the criteria should be executable and should double as living documentation. The fourth root is the safety-engineering tradition — hazard analysis, FMEA, and the assurance standards that govern medical and avionics software — which inverts the usual order and derives the specification from a systematic enumeration of failure modes rather than from the happy path.

The expert move is to notice that "must not miss" is not a criterion at all. It is a target without an observation procedure — no one could run it, and therefore no one could ever be shown to have failed it.

3Mechanics in depth, including the arithmetic

Expert practice begins with enumeration by mechanism rather than by imagination. You walk the core scenario one step at a time and ask, of each step, what it can return other than success. Each step has a bounded set of non-success returns: invalid input, unmet precondition, unauthorised actor, dependency refusal, dependency silence, duplicate arrival, limit breach, and stale state — the world moved while the request was in flight. This produces a repeatable list, which matters because imagination produces whatever the most anxious person in the room happens to fear, and varies between authors.

The step that separates practitioners is what happens next: each enumerated case is specified across four independent registers. What each party sees — and for a marketplace there are always at least two parties, whose screens must be consistent. What state the system lands in, including money, inventory or physical goods already committed. What is recorded, meaning the event and the metric by which the team will later learn the real incidence. And who is notified without having to go looking. These are genuinely independent; teams that collapse them into a single "show an error" sentence have specified roughly a quarter of the requirement.

There is a quantitative treatment, and experienced teams run it informally even when they do not write it down. For any enumerated error case, let λ be its expected annual incidence, c the expected all-in cost per incident (support handling, remediation, refunds, goodwill, and in regulated settings the cost of not being able to produce evidence), s the cost of specifying it — call it one loaded hour across product, engineering and quality, roughly ₹3,500 at Indian SaaS cost structures — and i the incremental implementation cost of the specified behaviour. 4When the idea applies, and when it misleads

The conditions can be stated as testable claims rather than principles. First: the requirement's outcome must be observable from outside the system. Prithula passes trivially — a passenger either received a replacement trip or did not. Pushpanjali passes for the deterministic wrapper (was an alert displayed, was the pharmacist's override recorded) and fails for the clinical core, because whether an interaction was clinically significant is a judgement made by qualified humans who disagree with one another at a measurable rate. That failure is not fatal; it changes the form of the criterion from a per-case assertion to a distributional one, which is the single most important adaptation on this page.

Second: the cost of being wrong must be borne by someone identifiable. Where it is not — where a defect degrades an aggregate slowly, as with a recommendation system that quietly narrows what customers see — acceptance criteria are the wrong instrument and will produce false comfort. Third: the specification must precede the commitment. A criterion written after an estimate is agreed cannot perform its main function.

The idea is actively misleading in two situations worth naming. The first is exploratory work where the purpose of the build is to discover what the requirement should be; imposing acceptance criteria on a prototype converts a learning exercise into a delivery commitment and destroys the option value that justified it. The second is any setting where passing the criteria is mistaken for the product being right. Kavya's team could hit recall, precision and latency targets exactly and still ship a feature that pharmacists learn to dismiss reflexively, at which point every criterion is met and the clinical benefit is zero. Acceptance criteria are a verdict instrument, never a judgement instrument.

5Hard edge cases

Two-sided systems. Every error case in a marketplace has at least two audiences whose interests diverge at the moment of the error. When a Prithula driver cancels, the passenger's screen and the driver's screen are showing the same event from opposite ends, and the specification must state both and assert their consistency. The subtle failure is not that one side is wrong but that the two sides become eventually consistent with a window of several seconds during which a passenger and a driver on a phone call to one another are reading contradictory text. Rohan's twenty-four cases included one that no single-sided product would ever generate: "the maximum permissible interval during which the two parties may see different trip status is three seconds, and neither party may be shown a terminal status until both can be."

Regulated products. In Pushpanjali's market the specification is not merely a development artefact; it becomes evidence. If a hospital chain is asked to demonstrate that its dispensing system behaves safely, the acceptance criteria and the records of their verification are what it produces. This changes two things. Criteria must be traceable — each one linked to the requirement above it and the test below it, so that a change eighteen months later can be shown to have been re-verified. And the error cases acquire a category absent elsewhere: what the system does when it cannot assess something must be distinguishable, in the record, from what it does when it has assessed and found nothing. Silence and a clean bill of health must never render identically.

Hardware plus software. When part of the system is a device in a warehouse, the error cases must include what it does when it cannot reach you, and for how long, and the criterion must be verified at the device rather than at the server. This is the subject of the third worked example below, and it is where software-trained product managers most reliably fail, because their instinct is that a fix can be shipped.

AI-native features. Kavya's frozen evaluation set contained 3,000 prescription events labelled by a panel of three clinical pharmacists, of which 214 carried a clinically significant interaction. The incumbent rules engine achieved recall of 71 per cent. The new model reached 92.4 per cent — catching 198 of the 214 and missing 16 — at precision of 61 per cent, raising 325 alerts in all, of which 127 were false. That alert rate is 10.8 per cent of prescriptions, inside the chain's stated tolerance of 12 per cent. None of those numbers can be converted into "must not miss." All of them can be converted into criteria. The deep point is that the error cases of an AI feature include being confidently wrong, a category that deterministic software does not have, and no criterion can eliminate it. What criteria can do is govern what surrounds it: that the system distinguishes "not assessed" from "assessed, nothing found"; that the pharmacist's override is recorded so the miss is discoverable later; that when the model is unavailable the system falls back to the rules engine and says so on screen.

Organisational seams. The error case that crosses two teams' backlogs has, in practice, no owner. Prithula's "payment captured, trip never started" belongs half to Rohan's marketplace team and half to the payments team in the same building, and in the first draft it appeared in neither backlog. Mature companies claim to solve this with cross-team design reviews. What they actually do, in the majority of cases, is discover it during an incident and then add an owner column to the error-case table — which is why an error-case list with a named human against each row is one of the more reliable signals that an organisation has been burned before.

6Nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The criterion is not the test, and the confusion is expensive in both directions

A criterion states what must be true; a test states how it will be checked, with what data, in which environment. One criterion may require eleven tests. The tell is a criterion that names a fixture — "using the test merchant account seeded with ₹5,000" — which reveals that the author has written a test and called it a criterion, and will therefore have to rewrite it every time the fixture changes.

Failure and silence are different outcomes, and the second is where incidents live

Most specifications model success and failure. Anything that crosses a network, a payment rail, a partner API or a device has three outcomes, the third being no answer at all. It is the only outcome in which the system's record and reality can diverge, and it is therefore the origin of nearly all reconciliation work. The expert tell is simple: read a PRD and look for the sentence beginning "if the other side does not respond". Its absence is a reliable indicator that the author has not personally operated a transactional system.

Every error case is a distributive policy wearing technical clothes

When a Prithula driver cancels and the replacement trip costs ₹210 more, someone pays: the passenger, the driver via a deduction, or Prithula. That is a commercial decision about which relationship the company will strain, and it is not an engineering choice. If the product manager does not make it in writing, it is made by default inside an exception handler by whoever is on shift. The obvious reading — that this is a detail to be settled during implementation — is wrong precisely because implementation is where policy becomes invisible.

Constrain the observable outcome, not the mechanism — with one real exception

"Retry three times with exponential backoff" is a design decision smuggled into a requirement. The correct form states outcome and deadline: no second debit, reconciled within ninety minutes. The exception matters and is often missed: where the mechanism is mandated externally by a regulator, a card scheme or a contract, the mechanism is the requirement. An expert can tell the two apart by asking whether an auditor would care how it was done, or only what resulted.

Completeness is unreachable; bounded incompleteness is the professional standard

The goal is not to enumerate every error case but to make the unspecified set explicit and bounded: specify the ranked few, state a default for everything else, and keep a short visible list of what was knowingly omitted, with owners. A named gap is a risk under management; an unnamed gap is an incident with a future date. The tell of an expert document is a section headed something like "deliberately not handled in v1" — a section that junior authors consider an admission of weakness and senior ones consider the point.

Criteria that describe the interface rather than the behaviour decay within a quarter

If a criterion would have to be rewritten because a designer moved a button, it is describing a screen. The diagnostic question is whether the criterion would survive a complete redesign. Screens change several times a year; behaviours change when policy changes, which is much less often. This is why the four-register formulation asks what the user sees rather than where on the page they see it.

Distributional criteria require a frozen artefact, or they mean nothing

"Recall at least 90 per cent" is meaningless without naming the set on which recall is measured, who labelled it, how disagreements among labellers were resolved, and how often it is refreshed. Kavya's set was frozen, jointly agreed with the customer, and scheduled for quarterly refresh with a rule that any refresh requires both parties' sign-off. Without that, the criterion floats: a team under pressure can meet it by changing the sample. The expert tell is asking, on hearing any model metric, "on what set?" — and noticing how often nobody in the room can answer.

Acceptance criteria answer "is it met", never "is it right"

A build can satisfy every criterion and be a commercial or clinical failure. Criteria are silent on whether the requirement was worth building, whether the experience is good rather than merely correct, and whether the feature interacts destructively with something shipped three years ago by a team that has since dissolved. Treating a green board as evidence of product success is among the most common category errors in delivery organisations, and it is more common in mature ones than in young ones because mature ones have better boards.

The number of blocking criteria is a governance choice, not a quality measure

Sixty criteria attached to a sign-off ritual detect less than nine criteria that someone actually reads. The expert distinguishes blocking criteria from documented non-blocking ones explicitly, and keeps the blocking set small enough that a human reads every line with attention. The tell of a decayed process is a sign-off sheet with many ticks and no annotations.

Timing determines function; the same sentence is a design tool or a weapon

Before estimation, criteria surface true scope and let a team commit knowingly. After the build, the identical words become the evidence in a dispute. Experienced practitioners guard the sequencing more fiercely than the wording, because wording can be improved later and sequencing cannot be recovered.

7How the practice differs by product type and stage

In consumer products, volumes are high and per-event value is low, so the dominant question is recovery without user action. The best consumer error handling is invisible: retry, reconcile, never show a code. Criteria concentrate on silent recovery, on the timing and wording of the one message that does reach the user, and on not blaming them. In enterprise, criteria are frequently contractual and are read adversarially by people paid to read them adversarially; permission and role errors dominate the error space, and the audit record is itself a criterion. In marketplaces the defining complication is the two audiences, discussed above. In hardware the defining complication is that the error case must be verified where the device is. In AI products the criteria split into distributional and absolute halves.

Where the difference is not real is worth saying plainly, because a great deal of writing on this topic implies otherwise. The enumeration method — walk the steps, ask what each can return other than success — is identical across all of these. The four registers are identical. The ranking arithmetic is identical. What changes is the mix of error cases the method surfaces and the form the criterion takes, not the method.

By stage the pathologies invert rather than diminish. Early-stage teams write too few criteria, which is usually a reasonable trade except on money-touching, irreversible and regulated paths, where it never is. Large organisations write too many and read none, and their characteristic failure is a thorough specification of the common cases with nothing said about the seams between teams — because the seams belong to nobody's document.

8Three worked examples, including one that failed

Pushpanjali Health Systems: converting a target into criteria

Kavya's team did not win the argument by explaining statistics. They won it by proposing an observation procedure. The criterion the parties eventually signed had four parts: on a frozen set of 3,000 prescription events jointly labelled by Pushpanjali's and the customer's pharmacists, recall on clinically significant interactions must be at least 90 per cent — against a measured 92.4 per cent, giving 2.4 points of headroom against a set that would be refreshed quarterly. The alert rate must not exceed 12 per cent of prescriptions — against a measured 10.8 per cent. Every alert must name the engine that produced it. And, in the part that took longest to draft, where any drug in a prescription is not present in the formulary mapping, the system must display "not assessed" in a visually distinct form and must never render that state identically to "no interaction found." The chief pharmacist signed it, because it gave her something she could check, and because the fourth clause addressed the hazard she actually feared: not that the machine would miss something, but that a pharmacist would read silence as safety.

Prithula Rides: pricing an error case before choosing a policy

Rohan's compensation decision came down to three options for the 7,680 annual post-departure cancellations. Doing nothing costs ₹0 directly and showed up as a measurable 14-day repeat-booking rate of 31 per cent among affected passengers against 58 per cent overall. Paying a flat ₹75 credit costs ₹5.76 lakh a year. Re-booking at price parity, which absorbs the median ₹210 premium, costs ₹16.1 lakh a year. Against that, the 27-point gap in repeat booking applied to 7,680 passengers at a contribution of ₹190 per subsequent trip implied roughly ₹3.9 lakh a year of foregone contribution in the first repeat alone, before any compounding. The numbers did not settle it, and Rohan did not pretend they had; what they did was convert a vague preference for generosity into a bounded question about retention elasticity that the data team could actually study.

Pushpavati Instruments: the acceptance criteria that were verified in the wrong place

Pushpavati Instruments makes cold-chain temperature loggers used by pharmaceutical distributors — a device in a consignment box reporting readings once a minute to a cloud service that produces the continuous temperature record a distributor must be able to show. The August 2025 release had a thorough specification: fourteen acceptance criteria on the ingestion path, covering duplicate readings, out-of-order arrival, clock skew and partial batches, all verified and all passing. The device's own behaviour when it could not reach the network was recorded in the PRD as "as per firmware default." The firmware default was a circular buffer of 2,000 readings, which at one per minute is 33 hours and 20 minutes.

In November a carrier configuration error left 380 devices without connectivity for 61 hours. Each lost the readings older than 33 hours: roughly 28 hours per device, 1,680 readings apiece. Sixty-one consignments could not produce a continuous record; nine, worth ₹47 lakh, were quarantined and ultimately written off. The failure was not in the code, which behaved exactly as designed, and not in the criteria, which passed. It was that every criterion was verified at the server, where the device's silence is indistinguishable from a device that had nothing to report.

The recovery was slower than the outage by two orders of magnitude. The firmware change — a larger buffer plus a store-and-forward acknowledgement so the device only discards a reading after the server confirms receipt — took four weeks to write and test. Deploying it took eleven weeks, because 640 of the 4,100 fielded devices ran an older bootloader that could not take an over-the-air update and required a physical visit at about ₹1,850 each, ₹11.8 lakh in all. For those eleven weeks distributors kept paper temperature logs. The durable change was not technical: Pushpavati's specification template now requires every error case to name the location at which the criterion is verified, and any case verified only in the cloud for a device-side behaviour is rejected at review.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

The first live disagreement is whether criteria must be executable. The specification-by-example position, in its strongest form, holds that any criterion not automated is a criterion nobody will check in a year, and that prose criteria decay into folklore while automated ones remain true by construction; the evidence is the observable fact that regression suites catch defects for years while requirement documents go stale within two releases. The context-driven testing tradition — James Bach, Michael Bolton — steelmans the opposite: scripted acceptance tests can only find what you thought of in advance, and an over-invested automated suite crowds out exploratory testing, which is the only activity that reliably finds the unimagined. For the first position to be wrong, it would have to be the case that automating criteria measurably reduces the discovery of unanticipated defects; for the second to be wrong, prose criteria would have to survive organisational turnover better than they demonstrably do.

The second is whether the verdict belongs before release or in production. The continuous-delivery position holds that a one per cent exposure with good instrumentation verifies more, faster and more cheaply than any pre-release gate, and that the gate is theatre inherited from an era when releases were expensive. The assurance position holds that this reasoning is valid only where errors are reversible and observable, and that its generalisation to medical, financial and physical-goods contexts is a category error: you cannot roll back a dispensed drug or an unrefrigerated consignment. Both are right within their domains, and the disagreement persists because each side generalises from a domain in which its answer is obviously correct.

The third is about authorship. One camp holds that acceptance criteria are product management's core written output and must be drafted by the person accountable for the outcome. Another — the three-amigos practice — holds that criteria drafted by one person encode one person's blind spots, and that the enumeration is materially better when product, engineering and testing do it together in one sitting. The empirical question, which the field has not settled, is whether the improvement in coverage is worth the coordination cost at scale; the honest answer appears to be that it is for requirements touching money, safety and irreversibility, and is not for the rest, but nobody has measured this well.

The fourth and least discussed is whether the error-case list should be ranked at all. The expected-value practice described in Exhibit 2 is standard in commercial software and close to forbidden in assurance-governed software, where the enumeration must be systematic and complete by construction rather than economic. Whether a hospital information platform should follow commercial or assurance practice is genuinely unsettled, and Kavya's team sits uncomfortably in the gap.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes good criteria for the requirement in front of them. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways. They enumerate mechanically rather than imaginatively, which means their error-case lists look similar across very different features because the method rather than the mood produced them. They rank before they specify, and can say out loud which cases they chose not to handle and why — and they override their own ranking, deliberately and with a stated reason, for cases that are irreversible, silent or regulatory. They ask where a criterion is observed, not merely what it asserts, which is the habit Pushpavati bought for ₹58.8 lakh. And they treat the specification as a negotiation instrument with a timing requirement, fighting to get criteria written before estimation rather than fighting about their wording afterwards.

There is a fifth, quieter mark. They read the artefacts other people produce in response to their omissions — support macros, reconciliation spreadsheets, the ops WhatsApp group where someone asks every Tuesday what to do about a particular state — as feedback on their own writing rather than as other teams' problems.

12What each decides

Kavya signed a four-part criterion in which the model's performance is distributional and measured against a frozen, jointly-labelled set, and the software around the model is held to absolute, per-case standards — with the abstention clause, the one that prevents silence from reading as safety, as the only clause she declared non-negotiable. UAT went ahead on 20 April against criteria both parties could run.

Rohan specified nine of his twenty-four error cases as blocking, documented eleven more with a hold-and-alert default, and promoted three low-expected-value cases — including the simultaneous double cancellation — into the blocking set on the explicit ground that their failure mode is silent rather than expensive. He took the estimate from eleven days to nineteen to his director with Exhibit 2 in hand, arguing that ₹105 lakh of expected annual cost was the relevant comparison to eight engineering days. On the compensation policy he committed only to a bounded experiment, on the reasoning that he had priced the error case but not yet measured the elasticity that would settle it.

Three questions for discussion. First: Kavya's criterion permits sixteen missed interactions in three thousand prescriptions. If you were the hospital chain's chief pharmacist, what would you need to see in the record — and from whom — before signing a number greater than zero? Second: Rohan overrode his own expected-value ranking for three cases. What rule would you write that promotes silent and irreversible failures without reopening the door to specifying everything? Third: Pushpavati's criteria all passed and its product failed. What would have to change in a specification review — not in the engineering — for that gap to be caught before a release rather than after?

13Going deeper

PRD structure is the container this sits in; criteria are what make the rest of the document checkable rather than aspirational, and a PRD's quality is largely determined by whether its requirements section can carry criteria at all. Edge cases, states and permissions extends the enumeration from failures to state machines and role-based behaviour, which is where enterprise error spaces actually live and where most of the unwritten cases hide. Requirements traceability is what keeps a criterion attached to the test that proves it when the feature is modified two years later, and is the mechanism by which regulated products survive change. Definition of done raises the level from a single requirement to the team's standing contract about what shipping means, absorbing the criteria that recur across every story. Specifying AI features develops the distributional half of section 5 into a full practice, including evaluation-set governance and what to do about confidently wrong output.

PM artefacts: one-pager, PRD, spec, strategy doc situates acceptance criteria in a family of documents and clarifies which arguments belong in which. Writing a one-pager matters because a criterion is only as good as the problem statement above it. Customer narratives (Day 0 / Day N) supply the lived sequence from which error cases are enumerated, and Day N narratives in particular surface the states that only appear after months of use. Telemetry requirements are the fourth register — recorded — treated as a first-class requirement, and without them the incidence figures in Exhibit 2 cannot exist. Non-functional requirements cover the criteria that attach to no single scenario, such as latency and availability, which is where the deadline half of an outcome-and-deadline criterion comes from. Release criteria and success metrics close the loop by separating "is this requirement met" from "was this worth doing" — the distinction this page has insisted on throughout.
